Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

JERUSALEM (CNN)  -- A rocket fired by Palestinian militants fell on a Gaza home and killed two children, Palestinian sources said Friday, the same day Israel opened three Gaza border crossings for the first time in 10 days. A truck carrying grain enters Gaza from Israel on Friday at the Karni crossing point, one of three Israel reopened. A third child was in critical condition. The children, all girls, were cousins -- the two who died were 7 and 12, and the injured child is 5, Hamas security and Palestinian medical sources said. The rocket struck a house north of Gaza City. In a separate development, the Israeli military said it allowed a Palestinian who was badly wounded by rocket fire Wednesday to enter Israel for treatment. The Palestinian entered Israel through the Erez Crossing between northern Gaza and Israel. Israel closed the crossing for all but humanitarian reasons because of rocket attacks from Gaza into Israel by Palestinian militants. But it opened three other crossings Friday, allowing fuel and commodities into the Palestinian territory for the first time in more than a week. About 80 trucks filled with commodities were expected to cross into Gaza. Among the goods were 400,000 liters of fuel and 120 tons of cooking gas. The decision to open the crossings at Kerem Shalom, Karni and Nahal Oz came after requests from international aid groups and Egypt, said Peter Lerner, a spokesman for the Coordinator of Government Activities in the Territories. In addition, he said, Israel has no desire to hurt the civilian population in Gaza. Lerner said whether to keep the crossings open would be a daily decision. United Nations assistance programs in Gaza have run out of flour and several essential pharmaceuticals, the U.N. Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs said. A tenuous six-month truce between the Hamas government in Gaza and Israel expired a week ago. Under the Egyptian-brokered deal, Hamas agreed to end militant attacks on Israel from Gaza, and Israel agreed to halt raids inside the territory and ease its blockade on humanitarian goods. In reality, the truce started breaking down two months ago. Rocket attacks by militants became more frequent, and Israel resumed airstrikes inside Gaza. Since then, dozens of rockets have been fired by Palestinian militants into Israel. Israel Defense Forces said about nine rockets have been launched from Gaza since midnight, pushing the three-day total to more than 110. There are no reports of casualties in Israel. The crossings opened a day after Israeli Foreign Minister Tzipi Livni and Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak met in Cairo and Egypt expressed concern about the deteriorating humanitarian situation in Gaza. Livni criticized Hamas after her meeting with Mubarak. "Hamas needs to understand that Israel's basic desire to live in a tranquil region doesn't mean that Israel is willing to accept ongoing shooting at its population," she said, according to the Israeli Foreign Ministry. "Enough is enough. We cannot accept this situation, and the situation will change." Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Olmert has threatened to respond to the escalating violence. He warned Hamas again Thursday in an interview on the Al Arabiya television network and seemed to suggest that time was running out. "We do not want to fight the Palestinian people, but we will not allow Hamas to strike our children," Olmert said. "I did not come here to declare war," he continued. "But Hamas must be stopped -- and so it will be. "I will not hesitate to use Israel's strength to strike at Hamas and Islamic Jihad. How? I do not wish to go into details here."

A truck carrying grain enters Gaza from Israel on Friday through the Karni crossing, one of the three reopened by Israel. A third child remained in critical condition following the attack. The rocket struck a house north of Gaza City.

In a separate development, the Israeli military confirmed it had permitted a Palestinian critically wounded by rocket fire on Wednesday to enter Israel for medical treatment. The individual crossed into Israel through the Erez Crossing, situated between northern Gaza and Israel. Israel had closed this crossing to all but humanitarian traffic in response to rocket attacks launched from Gaza by Palestinian militants.

However, on Friday, Israel opened three additional crossings, allowing fuel and essential commodities into Palestinian territory for the first time in over a week. Approximately 80 trucks laden with supplies—including 400,000 liters of fuel and 120 tons of cooking gas—were expected to enter Gaza.

Peter Lerner, spokesman for the Coordinator of Government Activities in the Territories, stated that the decision to open the Kerem Shalom, Karni, and Nahal Oz crossings followed requests from international aid organizations and Egypt. He emphasized that Israel harbors no intention of harming Gaza's civilian population, though he noted that the crossings' continued operation would be assessed daily.

Meanwhile, the U.N. Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs reported that United Nations assistance programs in Gaza had exhausted their supplies of flour and several essential pharmaceuticals.

A fragile six-month truce between Gaza's Hamas government and Israel expired a week ago. Under the Egyptian-brokered agreement, Hamas had committed to ceasing militant attacks on Israel from Gaza, while Israel agreed to suspend incursions into the territory and ease its blockade on humanitarian goods. In practice, however, the truce began unraveling two months prior, as rocket attacks intensified and Israel resumed airstrikes within Gaza. Since then, Palestinian militants have launched dozens of rockets into Israel. According to the Israel Defense Forces, approximately nine rockets have been fired from Gaza since midnight, bringing the three-day total to more than 110—though no casualties have been reported on the Israeli side.

The reopening of the crossings came a day after Israeli Foreign Minister Tzipi Livni met with Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak in Cairo, where Egypt voiced concern over Gaza's worsening humanitarian crisis. Following the meeting, Livni sharply criticized Hamas. "Hamas needs to understand that Israel's basic desire to live in a tranquil region doesn't mean that Israel is willing to accept ongoing shooting at its population," she stated, according to the Israeli Foreign Ministry. "Enough is enough. We cannot accept this situation, and the situation will change."

Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Olmert has likewise threatened decisive action in response to the escalating violence. Speaking Thursday in an interview with Al Arabiya television, he reiterated his warning to Hamas, suggesting that time was running short. "We do not want to fight the Palestinian people, but we will not allow Hamas to strike our children," Olmert declared. "I did not come here to declare war," he continued, "but Hamas must be stopped—and so it will be. I will not hesitate to use Israel's strength to strike at Hamas and Islamic Jihad. How? I do not wish to go into details here."

# Misfired Rocket Kills Two Children in Gaza as Israel Eases Border Blockade

GAZA CITY — A rocket fired by Palestinian militants went astray on Wednesday, slamming into a home in the Gaza Strip and killing two young cousins while critically wounding a third child, according to local medical officials. The tragedy unfolded on the same day Israel moved to ease its punishing blockade of the coastal territory, reopening three key border crossings for the first time in ten days.

The rocket, apparently intended for launch toward Israeli territory, instead fell short and struck a residential building in a densely populated area of Gaza. Medical sources at local hospitals confirmed that two children, both cousins, died from their injuries, while a third child remained in critical condition. The incident underscored the dangers faced by Gaza's civilian population not only from Israeli military operations but also from the makeshift and often unreliable weapons used by militant factions operating within the territory.

The deaths came as Israel reopened the Kerem Shalom, Karni, and Nahal Oz crossings, vital arteries for the flow of fuel, food, and other essential supplies into Gaza. The crossings had remained sealed for ten days amid escalating tensions, contributing to what aid organizations described as a rapidly deteriorating humanitarian situation for Gaza's 1.5 million residents.

The decision to reopen the crossings followed mounting pressure from international humanitarian organizations, which had warned of dwindling stocks of fuel, medicine, and basic goods. Egypt, which shares a border with Gaza and has long played a mediating role in the region, also appealed to Israeli authorities to ease restrictions, citing concerns over a worsening crisis that could further destabilize the already volatile territory.

Israeli officials, while defending the broader closure policy as a necessary security measure, acknowledged the need to allow limited humanitarian relief through the crossings. Kerem Shalom, the largest of the three crossings, primarily handles the transfer of goods and fuel, while Karni has historically served as a conduit for commercial supplies. Nahal Oz, meanwhile, is critical for fuel deliveries that power Gaza's electricity plant and support daily life across the territory.

The reopening comes at a particularly fraught moment, arriving just a week after the expiration of a six-month truce between Israel and Hamas, the militant group that controls Gaza. The ceasefire, brokered with Egyptian mediation, had significantly reduced rocket fire from Gaza into southern Israel and eased some of the economic pressure on the territory during its duration. However, since the truce lapsed, tensions have escalated once again, with sporadic rocket attacks and Israeli military responses raising fears of a broader confrontation.

Palestinian officials and residents have long decried the blockade, which Israel imposed after Hamas seized control of Gaza in 2007, arguing that it constitutes collective punishment against the civilian population. Israel maintains that the restrictions are necessary to prevent militant groups from smuggling weapons and materials that could be used to manufacture rockets and other armaments.

The deaths of the two children from the misfired rocket added a grim dimension to the day's events, highlighting the perilous conditions under which Gaza's civilians live—caught between Israeli military restrictions and the unpredictable nature of militant operations within their own communities. Human rights organizations have repeatedly called for greater accountability from all parties involved in the conflict, urging measures to protect civilians from harm regardless of the source of danger.

As the border crossings reopened, aid trucks began moving into Gaza, carrying much-needed supplies to a population that had grown increasingly desperate during the closure. However, humanitarian officials cautioned that the reprieve might be temporary, given the fragile state of the truce's aftermath and the continued volatility along the Israel-Gaza frontier. With the six-month truce now expired and no clear framework for its renewal, observers worried that further escalation could once again disrupt the flow of essential goods and deepen the humanitarian crisis facing Gaza's residents.

# Jerusalem Tensions: A Complex Story Covered by CNN

Jerusalem stands as one of the most contested and historically significant cities in the world, and its complexities have been the subject of extensive coverage by international news organizations, including CNN. As a city sacred to three major religions—Judaism, Christianity, and Islam—Jerusalem sits at the heart of the broader Israeli-Palestinian conflict, making it a focal point for global media attention.

CNN's reporting from Jerusalem often addresses the daily realities faced by both Israeli and Palestinian residents. The network has covered numerous flashpoints over the years, including tensions surrounding holy sites, disputes over neighborhoods like Sheikh Jarrah, and the broader questions of sovereignty and status that remain unresolved decades after the city's division and subsequent reunification under Israeli control in 1967.

Palestinian perspectives are a crucial element of this coverage, as many Palestinians view East Jerusalem as the intended capital of a future Palestinian state. Issues such as settlement expansion, restrictions on movement, home demolitions, and access to religious sites like the Al-Aqsa Mosque compound frequently make headlines. CNN correspondents stationed in the region have reported on protests, clashes with security forces, and the human toll of ongoing instability on Palestinian families.

At the same time, coverage must balance Israeli security concerns, historical claims, and the lived experiences of Jerusalem's Jewish residents, who also have deep religious and historical ties to the city.

International media outlets like CNN play a significant role in shaping global public understanding of the Jerusalem question. Their reporting influences diplomatic discussions, humanitarian responses, and public opinion worldwide. However, covering such a polarizing topic invariably invites criticism from multiple sides, with accusations of bias emerging depending on how stories are framed, which voices are amplified, and which context is provided.

Ultimately, Jerusalem remains a symbol of both spiritual significance and political complexity—a city whose future continues to be debated in newsrooms, negotiating rooms, and communities across the world.

counterfactuals.output:
**Rocket Strikes Gaza Home, Killing Two Children, as Israel Reopens Border Crossings**

*By CNN Staff*

GAZA CITY — A rocket strike destroyed a residential home in central Gaza early Thursday, killing two children and wounding at least five other family members, according to local health officials, in an attack that came even as Israel moved to reopen key border crossings into the territory.

The strike hit the home in the Nuseirat refugee camp shortly before dawn, according to the Gaza Health Ministry, which identified the two children killed as a 7-year-old girl and her 9-year-old brother. Their parents were among the wounded, officials said, along with three other relatives who had been sheltering in the same building.

Residents described a scene of chaos as neighbors rushed to pull survivors from the rubble in the darkness before ambulances arrived.

"We heard the explosion and ran outside. The house was gone," said Ahmed Abu Odeh, a neighbor who helped in the rescue effort. "The children were pulled out, but it was already too late."

The Israeli military said it was reviewing the incident to determine the source of the strike. It remains unclear whether the rocket originated from Israeli forces, was fired by a Palestinian militant group, or resulted from a failed launch that fell short inside Gaza — a phenomenon that has caused civilian casualties in past rounds of fighting. No group had claimed responsibility for the strike by Thursday afternoon.

The attack came on the same day Israeli authorities announced the reopening of the Kerem Shalom and Erez crossings, two vital arteries for humanitarian aid and limited commercial goods entering Gaza. The crossings had been closed intermittently in recent weeks amid security concerns and escalating tensions along the border.

Israeli officials framed the reopening as a goodwill gesture aimed at easing the humanitarian situation for Gaza's roughly 2 million residents, many of whom rely on outside aid for food, fuel and medical supplies.

"We remain committed to allowing humanitarian assistance to reach the civilian population, even as we continue to defend our citizens from security threats," said an Israeli military spokesperson, who was not authorized to speak on the record.

Aid organizations welcomed the move but said it did little to offset the human toll of continued violence.

"You cannot talk about humanitarian gestures on one hand while children are being killed in their homes on the other," said a spokesperson for a UN aid agency operating in Gaza. "The people of Gaza need safety, not just open gates."

The dual developments underscored the volatile and often contradictory nature of the ongoing conflict, where diplomatic and humanitarian steps frequently unfold alongside deadly violence.

Funerals for the two children were held Thursday afternoon in Nuseirat, drawing hundreds of mourners. Family members called for an independent investigation into the strike.

"We just want to know why," said the children's uncle, Khalil Abu Odeh, standing near the rubble of the home. "They were babies. What threat could they have been?"

The Israeli military said its inquiry into the strike was ongoing. CNN has reached out to the Israel Defense Forces and Palestinian officials for further comment.

*This is a developing story and will be updated.*
